intro: Across India and East Asia, people light lamps, ring bells, share free meals and bow to their grandparents. These actions come from some of the oldest traditions in the world. Millions of people follow them today, including many families in Chicago.

In this unit you will meet Hinduism and Buddhism, then Sikhism, Jainism, and the teachings of Confucius and the Dao. You will learn their stories, words, holidays and practices. You will see what adherents believe and why their practices matter to them.
By the end, you will be able to explain key words, match practices to traditions and compare how each tradition teaches people to live well. You will describe each one fairly, in its own words.
bigQuestion: How do traditions from India and East Asia teach people to live a good life?

title: Traditions of India and East Asia

chapters.title: Hinduism and Buddhism
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Hindus and Buddhists describe a good life, and what practices help them live it?

story.title: A Lamp and a Bell
story.kicker: Two Chicago kids, two traditions, and one autumn week full of light and sound.
paragraphs: It is a cool night in October. Arjun kneels by the front window of his family's apartment. He holds a small clay lamp called a diya. His grandmother pours in a little oil and helps him light the wick. Soon a row of tiny flames glows along the sill.

"Why do we light so many?" Arjun asks. His grandmother smiles. She says many Hindus light lamps at Diwali to remember that light wins over darkness. She tells him the story of Prince Rama coming home. The people lit lamps to welcome him back.

A few miles away, on the North Side of Chicago, Mai walks into a Buddhist temple with her mother. The room is quiet. It smells of incense. A calm statue of the Buddha sits at the front, with flowers and fruit placed before it.

Mai takes a soft mallet and taps a large bowl-shaped bell. A low hum fills the room and slowly fades. Her mother tells her the sound can help people stop, breathe and pay attention. Then they sit together in silence for a few minutes.

Arjun and Mai follow different traditions. Both traditions began long ago in India. Both have stories, teachers and practices. In this chapter you will learn how Hindus and Buddhists describe the world and how they try to live well in it.
story.think: Arjun's family uses light and Mai's family uses sound. What might each one help a person notice or remember?

lessons.title: One Tradition, Many Ways
lessons.mainIdea: Hinduism is a very old tradition from India with many ways to worship and many sacred texts.
reading: Hinduism began in India more than 3,000 years ago. It has no single founder. It grew over many centuries from many teachers, songs and customs. Today about 1.2 billion people are Hindu. Most live in India and Nepal. Many also live in the United States, including Chicago.

Hindus have many sacred texts. The oldest are the *Vedas*, collections of hymns and teachings. Later texts include the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita. Great story poems, like the Ramayana, are loved by families. Children often hear these stories from parents and grandparents.

Hindus do not all worship the same way. Some honor Vishnu most. Some honor Shiva. Some honor a goddess, called Devi. Many Hindus call their way of life *Sanatana Dharma*, which means "the eternal way." Scholars say Hinduism is really a family of related paths.

words.d: the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, made up of hymns and teachings
a name many Hindus use for their tradition; it means "the eternal way"

look.title: Picture a Family Shelf
look.text: Picture a shelf in a Hindu family's home. On it sits a small statue of Ganesha, who has an elephant head. Next to it is a picture of Krishna playing a flute. A small book of the Bhagavad Gita rests nearby. A bell and a tiny lamp sit in front.
look.prompt: Why might one family keep more than one sacred image on the same shelf?

check.q: Where did Hinduism begin?
check.why: Hinduism began in India more than 3,000 years ago.

check.q: What are the Vedas?
choices: the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism
check.why: The Vedas are collections of hymns and teachings, the oldest Hindu texts.

check.q: Why do scholars call Hinduism a family of paths?
choices: Hindus worship in many different ways
check.why: Hindus honor different deities and follow different customs, so scholars see many related paths.

lessons.title: Many Gods and One Spirit
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus describe many gods and goddesses as faces of one great spirit, called Brahman.
reading: Hindu temples hold many images. There is Ganesha, who many Hindus say removes obstacles. There is Lakshmi, linked to good fortune. There is Shiva, the dancer. Each image is called a *murti*. Hindus believe the deity can be present in the murti during worship.

Many Hindus also speak of *Brahman*. In the Upanishads, Brahman is the one great spirit behind everything. Many Hindus teach that the many gods are different faces of this one reality. It is a little like one person being a parent, a teacher and a friend.

Not every Hindu explains this the same way. Some Hindus focus on one god as supreme. Others focus on Brahman beyond any image. Hindu teachers have discussed these ideas for centuries. Students can describe these views without deciding which one is right.

words.d: in Hindu teaching, the one great spirit or reality behind everything
a sacred image or statue of a Hindu deity used in worship

look.title: A Teaching from the Vedas
look.text: Truth is one. The wise call it by many names.
look.cite: Rig Veda 1.164.46, a well-known Hindu teaching, in our own words
look.prompt: How could this line help explain why Hindus use many names for the divine?

check.q: In the Upanishads, what is Brahman?
choices: the one great spirit behind everything
check.why: The Upanishads describe Brahman as the one reality behind all things.

check.q: What is a murti?
choices: a sacred image of a deity used in worship
check.why: A murti is an image of a deity; many Hindus believe the deity is present in it during worship.

check.q: Which statement is the most accurate?
choices: Hindus explain the one and the many in different ways
Hindus believe there are no gods
check.why: Hindu views vary: some focus on one god, others on Brahman beyond images.

lessons.title: Worship at Home and Temple
lessons.mainIdea: Puja is Hindu worship with offerings, light and prayer, done at home and in temples.
reading: Many Hindu homes have a small shrine. Each morning, a family member may do *puja*. Puja means worship. The person offers flowers, fruit, water or incense to the murti. They may ring a bell and wave a lamp in circles. They often say or sing a prayer.

Hindus also worship in a *mandir*, or temple. A priest leads puja there. People bring offerings and receive a blessing. Many Hindus take off their shoes before going in. There are Hindu temples in the Chicago area, such as in Lemont and Aurora.

Water is sacred in Hindu tradition. The Ganges River in India is especially holy to Hindus. They call it Ganga Ma, or Mother Ganga. Millions of pilgrims bathe in it. Many Hindus believe its water washes away wrongdoing.

words.d: Hindu worship with offerings such as flowers, food, light and prayer
a Hindu temple
a person who travels to a holy place for religious reasons

look.title: Steps of a Home Puja
look.text: A girl washes her hands. She places a marigold in front of a small murti. She lights a small lamp and moves it in slow circles. She rings a little bell. Then she folds her hands, bows her head, and says a short prayer.
look.prompt: Which of these steps use the senses of sight, smell, sound or touch?

check.q: What does puja mean?
check.why: Puja is Hindu worship with offerings and prayer.

check.q: Which river is especially sacred to Hindus?
check.why: Hindus call the Ganges Ganga Ma and many bathe in it as pilgrims.

check.q: What is a mandir?
check.why: A mandir is a Hindu temple where a priest leads puja.

lessons.title: Diwali and Holi
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali celebrates light over darkness, and Holi welcomes spring with colors.
reading: *Diwali* is the Hindu festival of lights. It comes in October or November. Families light rows of lamps and hang lights. They clean their homes, wear new clothes and share sweets. Many honor Lakshmi. Many remember the story of Rama coming home.

*Holi* comes in the spring, often in March. People throw bright colored powder and water at each other. Friends and strangers laugh together. Many Hindus tell the story of young Prahlad, whose faith kept him safe. Holi also welcomes the warm season.

Hindu festivals follow a calendar based on the moon. So the dates change each year on the school calendar. In Chicago, families celebrate at home and at temples. Some schools and parks hold Diwali events too. Sikhs and Jains also mark Diwali, for their own reasons.

words.d: the Hindu festival of lights, celebrated in autumn
a spring Hindu festival celebrated with colored powder and water

look.title: When Hindu Festivals Come
look.cite: common calendars; dates move each year
look.prompt: Which festival usually comes first in the school year that starts in August?

check.q: What do many Hindus celebrate at Diwali?
check.why: Diwali is the festival of lights; lamps stand for light over darkness.

check.q: What makes Holi easy to recognize?
choices: bright colored powder thrown in fun
check.why: At Holi, people throw colored powder and water to welcome spring.

check.q: Why do Diwali dates change each year?
choices: The date is chosen by the President
check.why: The Hindu calendar is based on the moon, so dates shift on the school calendar.

lessons.title: Karma: Actions Matter
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus teach karma, the idea that every action brings results.
reading: Imagine planting a seed. A sunflower seed grows a sunflower, not a tomato. Many Hindus use this picture for *karma*. Karma means action. Hindus teach that good actions bring good results and harmful actions bring harmful results.

Hindus also speak of *dharma*. Dharma is duty, the right way to live. A student's dharma may be to study and respect teachers. A parent's dharma may be to care for the family. Many Hindus believe that doing your dharma well creates good karma.

The Bhagavad Gita is a famous Hindu text. In it, the god Krishna teaches the warrior Arjuna. Krishna tells him to do his duty without worrying about rewards. Many Hindus read the Gita for advice about how to act well.

words.d: action; in Hindu and Buddhist teaching, the idea that actions bring results
duty, the right way to live

look.title: Krishna's Advice
look.text: Do your work, but do not work only for the reward. Do not stop doing your duty either.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.47, Krishna speaking to Arjuna, in our own words
look.prompt: What does Krishna say a person should focus on: the action or the reward?

check.q: What does karma mean?
choices: action, and the idea that actions bring results
check.why: Karma means action; Hindus teach actions bring results.

check.q: What is dharma?
choices: duty, the right way to live
check.why: Dharma is duty; each person has a right way to live.

check.q: In the Bhagavad Gita, who teaches Arjuna?
check.why: In the Gita, Krishna teaches the warrior Arjuna about duty.

lessons.title: The Circle of Lives
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus believe the soul is reborn many times until it reaches moksha, freedom.
reading: Many Hindus believe each person has a soul, called the *atman*. They believe the body dies but the atman does not. The atman is born again in a new body. This is called *reincarnation*. Karma helps shape the next life, Hindus teach.

The Bhagavad Gita compares this to clothing. A person takes off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones. In the same way, the Gita says, the soul leaves an old body and takes a new one. This picture helps many Hindus think about death calmly.

Hindus teach that the circle of births does not have to go on forever. The goal is *moksha*, which means freedom. Many Hindus believe moksha comes through devotion, wisdom or good action. Different Hindu paths stress different ways.

words.d: in Hindu teaching, a person's soul or true self
the belief that a soul is born again in a new body after death
in Hindu teaching, freedom from the circle of rebirth

look.title: Old Clothes, New Clothes
look.text: As a person throws away worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the soul leaves worn-out bodies and enters new ones.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.22, in our own words
look.prompt: What does the clothing picture say stays the same and what changes?

check.q: What is the atman?
choices: a person's soul or true self
check.why: In Hindu teaching the atman is the soul, which Hindus believe is reborn.

check.q: What is moksha?
choices: freedom from the circle of rebirth
check.why: Hindus describe moksha as the goal: freedom from rebirth.

check.q: In the Gita's picture, what are the worn-out clothes like?
check.why: The Gita compares old clothes to old bodies the soul leaves behind.

lessons.title: Prince Siddhartha
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists tell how Prince Siddhartha left his palace to find the answer to suffering.
reading: Buddhists tell the story of Siddhartha Gautama. He was born a prince in South Asia, about 2,500 years ago. Scholars date his life to around 500 BCE. His father kept him inside a beautiful palace. The prince had everything he wanted.

One day Siddhartha rode outside the palace. The story says he saw an old man, a sick man and a dead body. He learned that everyone grows old, gets sick and dies. Then he saw a calm monk. Siddhartha decided to leave home and search for peace.

He studied with teachers and went without food for a long time. It did not bring him the answer. Then he sat under a tree to meditate. Buddhists believe he reached *enlightenment* there. From then on, he was called the *Buddha*, which means "the awakened one."

words.d: a title meaning "the awakened one"; used for Siddhartha Gautama
in Buddhism, waking up to the truth about life and suffering

look.title: Four Sights
look.text: In the story, Siddhartha sees four people outside the palace: an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a peaceful monk. The first three show him that life brings suffering. The fourth gives him an idea of what to do.
look.prompt: Why do you think the story puts the calm monk last?

check.q: What does the word Buddha mean?
check.why: Buddha is a title meaning the awakened one.

check.q: In the story, what did Siddhartha NOT see outside the palace?
check.why: The four sights were an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a monk.

check.q: Where do Buddhists say Siddhartha reached enlightenment?
choices: sitting under a tree in meditation
check.why: Buddhists teach he became the Buddha while meditating under a tree.

lessons.title: The Four Noble Truths
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha taught that craving causes suffering and that a path can end it.
reading: After his enlightenment, the Buddha began to teach. His first teaching was about the *Four Noble Truths*. Buddhists often compare him to a doctor. A doctor names the illness, finds the cause, says it can be cured and gives medicine.

The first truth is that life includes suffering. The second is that suffering comes from craving, or wanting things too much. The third is that suffering can end. Buddhists call this ending *nirvana*. The fourth truth is that there is a path to follow.

Think of wanting a new toy so much that you feel upset. Buddhists say craving works like that, but bigger. It can make people unhappy even when they have a lot. The Buddha taught a middle way, not too much and not too little.

words.d: the Buddha's first teaching: suffering, its cause, its end and the path
in Buddhism, the end of suffering and craving
wanting something too much

look.title: A Line from the Dhammapada
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought.
look.cite: Dhammapada, verse 1, tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: According to this line, where does a person's life begin to take shape?

check.q: What does the second Noble Truth name as the cause of suffering?
check.why: The second truth says suffering comes from craving.

check.q: What is nirvana?
choices: the end of suffering and craving
check.why: Buddhists describe nirvana as the end of suffering.

check.q: Why do Buddhists compare the Buddha to a doctor?
choices: He named the problem, its cause, and a cure
check.why: The Four Noble Truths move like a doctor: illness, cause, cure, medicine.

lessons.title: The Eightfold Path
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists follow the Eightfold Path of wise seeing, kind acting and careful minds.
reading: The fourth Noble Truth is a path. Buddhists call it the *Eightfold Path*. It has eight parts. It is often drawn as a wheel with eight spokes. The wheel reminds Buddhists that all eight parts work together.

Some parts are about wisdom, like seeing clearly. Some are about acting well. These include right speech, right action and right livelihood, or honest work. Other parts train the mind. These include effort, mindfulness and concentration.

Many Buddhists also keep five basic precepts, or promises. They promise not to kill, not to steal, not to lie, not to misuse the senses and not to take intoxicants. Monks and nuns keep many more rules.

words.d: the Buddha's path of eight parts for ending suffering
a promise or rule for living; Buddhists keep five basic precepts

look.title: The Dharma Wheel
look.text: Look at a wheel with eight spokes. It is the symbol of Buddhism, called the Dharma wheel. Each spoke stands for one part of the Eightfold Path. If one spoke breaks, the wheel wobbles.
look.prompt: What might a wobbly wheel teach about keeping only some parts of the path?

check.q: How many parts does the Buddha's path have?
check.why: It is called the Eightfold Path because it has eight parts.

check.q: Which is one of the five basic Buddhist precepts?
check.why: The five precepts include not killing, stealing or lying.

check.q: What symbol shows the Eightfold Path?
check.why: The Dharma wheel's eight spokes stand for the eight parts.

lessons.title: Monks, Temples and Meditation
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists meditate, visit temples and support monks and nuns who study the Buddha's teaching.
reading: Many Buddhists practice *meditation*. They sit still and pay close attention. Some watch their breath going in and out. Some repeat kind wishes for all beings. Buddhists teach that meditation can calm and train the mind.

The Buddhist community includes *monks* and nuns. They shave their heads and wear simple robes. In some countries, the robes are orange or saffron. Many live in monasteries. Families bring them food, and the monks teach and chant.

Buddhist temples are often quiet places. People bow to the Buddha image. They offer flowers, candles and incense. The flowers wilt, which reminds Buddhists that everything changes. Chicago has many Buddhist temples from many countries.

words.d: training the mind by sitting still and paying close attention
a man who leaves ordinary life to live by religious rules, often in a monastery

look.title: Flowers That Fade
look.text: At a Buddhist temple, a woman places fresh flowers in front of the Buddha image. A week later the flowers have turned brown. A teacher says this is not sad. It is a lesson that everything changes.
look.prompt: What lesson do the fading flowers teach to many Buddhists?

check.q: What do many Buddhists do in meditation?
choices: sit still and pay close attention
check.why: Meditation means training the mind by paying close attention.

check.q: Why might flowers be offered at a Buddhist temple?
choices: Their fading reminds people that everything changes
check.why: Buddhists see wilting flowers as a lesson in change.

check.q: Who brings food to monks in many Buddhist lands?
check.why: Lay families support monks with food; monks teach and chant.

lessons.title: Two Big Branches
lessons.mainIdea: Theravada and Mahayana are two big branches of Buddhism found in different lands.
reading: Buddhism spread from India to many lands. Over time it grew into branches. *Theravada* means "the way of the elders." It is common in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia. It stresses the monks and the oldest teachings.

*Mahayana* means "the great vehicle." It is common in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Many Mahayana Buddhists honor bodhisattvas. A bodhisattva is a being who helps others reach enlightenment. Zen and Pure Land are Mahayana schools.

Tibetan Buddhism is another major form. Its best-known teacher is the Dalai Lama. Today about 500 million people are Buddhist, by common estimates. Most live in Asia. Chicago has Thai, Japanese, Vietnamese, Tibetan and other Buddhist temples.

words.d: "the way of the elders"; a branch of Buddhism common in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
"the great vehicle"; a branch of Buddhism common in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam
in Mahayana Buddhism, a being who helps others reach enlightenment

look.title: Where Many Buddhists Live
look.cite: common estimates, Pew Research Center 2010; counts vary widely
look.prompt: Which country has the most Buddhists? Why might counts in China be hard to make?

check.q: Which branch is common in Thailand and Sri Lanka?
check.why: Theravada, the way of the elders, is common in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

check.q: What is a bodhisattva?
choices: a being who helps others reach enlightenment
check.why: Mahayana Buddhists honor bodhisattvas who help others.

check.q: Zen is a school in which branch?
check.why: Zen and Pure Land are Mahayana schools.

lessons.title: Vesak and Comparing Paths
lessons.mainIdea: Vesak honors the Buddha, and Hindus and Buddhists share some words but explain them differently.
reading: *Vesak* is a major Buddhist holiday. It often falls in May, at a full moon. Many Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death on this day. They visit temples, light lanterns and give gifts to the poor. In some places, people free caged birds.

Hindus and Buddhists both come from ancient India. They share some words, like karma, dharma and rebirth. But they use them in different ways. For example, many Hindus teach there is a lasting soul, the atman. The Buddha taught that there is no unchanging self.

Both traditions offer practices to live well. Hindus may do puja and follow their dharma. Buddhists may meditate and follow the Eightfold Path. Scholars compare these carefully. They describe each tradition in its own words.

words.d: a Buddhist holiday honoring the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death
being born again after death; Hindus and Buddhists explain it differently

look.title: Same Word, Two Meanings
look.text: A Hindu student says, "My dharma is my duty as a student." A Buddhist student says, "The Dharma is the teaching of the Buddha." Both use the same word. Each means something a little different.
look.prompt: How could you ask a friend what a word means in their tradition?

check.q: Which holiday honors the Buddha's birth and enlightenment?
check.why: Vesak remembers the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death.

check.q: How do Hindu and Buddhist teachings about the self differ?
choices: Buddhists teach the atman; Hindus deny it
Many Hindus teach a lasting soul; the Buddha taught no unchanging self
check.why: Hindus speak of the atman; the Buddha taught there is no unchanging self.

check.q: Which word do Hindus and Buddhists both use?
check.why: Both traditions use karma, though they explain it in their own ways.

review.q: Which tradition calls itself Sanatana Dharma, the eternal way?
review.why: Many Hindus use this name for their tradition.

review.q: A family waves a lamp and offers flowers to a murti. What is this?
review.why: Puja is Hindu worship with offerings and light.

review.q: Which festival is called the festival of lights?
review.why: Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights.

review.q: What do many Hindus call freedom from rebirth?
review.why: Moksha is the Hindu word; nirvana is the Buddhist term for the end of suffering.

review.q: What do Buddhists say Siddhartha became under the tree?
review.why: Buddhists teach he reached enlightenment and became the Buddha.

review.q: According to the Four Noble Truths, what causes suffering?
review.why: The second Noble Truth names craving as the cause.

review.q: Which branch of Buddhism is common in Japan and Korea?
review.why: Mahayana is common in East Asia.

review.q: In the Bhagavad Gita, what does Krishna teach Arjuna to do?
choices: leave home and become a monk
do his duty without working only for reward
review.why: Krishna urges Arjuna to do his duty and not act only for rewards.

chapters.title: Sikhism, Jainism, Confucius and the Dao
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Sikhs, Jains, Confucians and Daoists each teach people to treat others and the world?

story.title: Everyone Sits on the Floor
story.kicker: At a Sikh gurdwara, a free meal teaches a lesson about who is equal.
paragraphs: It is Sunday morning at a gurdwara in the Chicago suburbs. A gurdwara is a Sikh house of worship. Priya's family takes off their shoes at the door. Everyone covers their head with a scarf or a turban. Priya ties a bright blue scarf over her hair.

Inside, people listen to hymns sung from a large book resting under a cloth canopy. Then they walk to a big hall. Long mats cover the floor. Volunteers are carrying pots of lentils, rice and warm flatbread called roti.

A man in a business suit sits down. Next to him sits a woman who just finished a night shift. A family visiting for the first time sits down too. Nobody has a better seat. Everyone sits on the floor in rows and is served the same food.

Priya's job today is to hand out roti. "Why is it free?" asks a visitor. Priya grins. "This is langar," she says. "Guru Nanak taught that everyone is equal. So everyone eats together, and anyone is welcome."
In this chapter you will meet four traditions. Sikhs share the langar. Jains try to harm no living thing. Followers of Confucius honor family and teachers. Daoists try to live in harmony with nature.
story.think: Why might sitting on the same floor matter more than just giving people free food?

lessons.title: Guru Nanak's Message
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs follow the teachings of Guru Nanak, who taught one God and the equality of all people.
reading: Sikhism began in the Punjab region of South Asia about 500 years ago. Its first teacher was *Guru Nanak*, born in 1469. Sikhs tell that as a young man he went into a river and was gone for three days. When he came back, he said, "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim."

Sikhs understand this to mean that God sees all people as one family. Guru Nanak taught that there is one God. He taught that all people are equal, whatever their religion, caste or gender. A *Guru* is a teacher. Sikhs honor ten human Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh.

The word Sikh means learner or student. Sikhs try to remember God, work honestly and share with others. Today there are about 25 to 30 million Sikhs. Most live in India. Many live in Canada, Britain and the United States.

words.d: a teacher; Sikhs honor ten human Gurus and their holy book as Guru
a follower of Sikhism; the word means learner

look.title: The Opening of the Sikh Scripture
look.text: There is one Creator. Truth is its name. It is without fear and without hate. It is timeless and was never born.
look.cite: Mul Mantar, opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, by Guru Nanak, in our own words
look.prompt: What words in this line describe what Sikhs believe about God?

check.q: Who was the first Sikh Guru?
check.why: Guru Nanak, born in 1469, was the first Guru.

check.q: What does the word Sikh mean?
check.why: Sikh means learner.

check.why: Guru Nanak taught one God and the equality of all people.

lessons.title: The Gurdwara and the Langar
lessons.mainIdea: In the gurdwara, Sikhs sing from their holy book and share a free meal called langar.
reading: A *gurdwara* is a Sikh house of worship. The name means "door of the Guru." Inside is the holy book, the *Guru Granth Sahib*. Sikhs treat it as their living Guru. It rests on a raised seat under a canopy. Hymns from it are sung with music.

Every gurdwara has a *langar*. Langar is a free kitchen and meal. Volunteers cook and serve. Anyone may eat, whether Sikh or not. People usually sit on the floor together. This shows that no one is higher than anyone else.

Visitors are welcome in gurdwaras. They cover their heads and take off their shoes. They do not bring tobacco or alcohol. The Golden Temple in Amritsar, India, is the most famous gurdwara. Its langar serves many thousands of people each day.

words.d: a Sikh house of worship; the name means door of the Guru
the Sikh holy book, which Sikhs honor as their living Guru
the free meal and kitchen at every gurdwara, open to all

look.title: Serving Langar
look.text: A volunteer rolls roti. Another stirs lentils. A girl pours water for guests. An old man washes dishes. None of them is paid. Sikhs call this seva, which means selfless service.
look.prompt: Why might Sikhs see washing dishes as part of their religion?

check.q: What is langar?
choices: a free meal open to everyone
check.why: Langar is the free kitchen and meal in every gurdwara.

check.q: How do Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib?
choices: as a storybook for children only
check.why: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as their Guru.

check.q: Why do people sit on the floor at langar?
choices: because chairs are forbidden in India
to show no one is higher than anyone else
because it is a Hindu rule
check.why: Sitting together shows the Sikh teaching of equality.

lessons.title: The Turban and the Five Ks
lessons.mainIdea: Many Sikhs keep five articles of faith, called the five Ks, and wear a turban.
reading: In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh started the *Khalsa*. The Khalsa is the community of initiated Sikhs. Members promise to keep five articles of faith. Each begins with the letter K in Punjabi. They are called the five Ks.

The five Ks are: kesh, uncut hair; kangha, a small wooden comb; kara, a steel bracelet; kachera, cotton undershorts; and kirpan, a small sword. Sikhs explain each one. The kara's circle reminds them God has no beginning or end. The kirpan stands for protecting others.

Many Sikh men, and some Sikh women, wear a *turban* over their uncut hair. The turban is a sign of faith and dignity. Sikhs in America sometimes face teasing about it. Kind classmates ask respectful questions instead.

words.d: five articles of faith kept by initiated Sikhs, each starting with K in Punjabi
a long cloth wrapped around the head; for many Sikhs a sign of faith
the community of initiated Sikhs, begun in 1699

look.title: A New Classmate

check.why: The kara is one of the five Ks, a steel bracelet.

check.why: Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five Ks.

lessons.title: Mahavira and Ahimsa
lessons.mainIdea: Jains follow Mahavira's teaching of ahimsa, doing no harm to any living thing.
reading: Jainism is an ancient tradition from India. Jains honor 24 great teachers called *Tirthankaras*. The most recent was *Mahavira*. He lived in India about 2,500 years ago, around the same time as the Buddha. He left his home to live a very simple life.

The heart of Jain teaching is *ahimsa*. Ahimsa means non-violence, doing no harm. Jains believe every living thing has a soul, even tiny insects. So they try hard not to hurt any being. They see ahimsa in actions, words and even thoughts.
There are about 4 to 5 million Jains today, by common estimates. Most live in India. Some live in the Chicago area. The Jain Society of Metropolitan Chicago has a temple in Bartlett.

words.d: non-violence; doing no harm to any living being
the most recent of the 24 great Jain teachers, who lived about 2,500 years ago
one of the 24 great teachers honored by Jains

look.title: A Jain Teaching
look.text: All living beings love their life. They want to be happy and do not want pain. So a person should not harm or kill any of them.
look.cite: Acaranga Sutra 1.2.3, a Jain scripture, in our own words
look.prompt: What reason does this teaching give for not harming living things?

check.why: Ahimsa means doing no harm to any living being.

check.why: Jains honor Mahavira as the 24th Tirthankara.

check.q: Why do Jains try not to hurt insects?

check.why: Jains teach that all living beings have souls.

lessons.title: Living Gently
lessons.mainIdea: Jains practice ahimsa in daily life through careful eating, speaking and working.
reading: Jains show ahimsa in many small ways. Most Jains are vegetarian. Many also avoid root vegetables, like onions and potatoes. Pulling up roots can kill tiny living things in the soil, Jains explain. Many do not eat after sunset.

Jain monks and nuns are extra careful. Some carry a soft broom to gently sweep insects from their path. Some wear a cloth over their mouth. This keeps them from breathing in tiny insects. They walk from place to place instead of riding.
Jains keep other vows too. They try to tell the truth, not steal, and not own too much. Not owning too much is called aparigraha. Jains teach that holding things lightly helps the soul become free.

words.d: a person who does not eat meat
a serious promise
the Jain vow of not owning or wanting too much

look.title: A Jain Lunch

look.prompt: Which parts of this lunch connect to ahimsa? Explain one.

check.q: What is aparigraha?

check.why: Aparigraha is the Jain vow of non-possessiveness.

lessons.title: Compare: Ahimsa and Karma
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus, Buddhists and Jains all speak of karma and non-harm, but in their own ways.
reading: Jainism, Hinduism and Buddhism all began in India. All three use the word karma. Jains explain karma in a special way. They describe it as fine matter that sticks to the soul. Harmful acts add more. Kind acts and self-control help clear it away.

All three traditions honor ahimsa too. Many Hindus and Buddhists are vegetarian for this reason. Jains usually make ahimsa the most central rule of all. Mahatma Gandhi, a Hindu, learned from Jain ideas. He used non-violence to work for India's freedom.

Scholars compare traditions by asking the same question of each. For example: What happens because of what we do? Each tradition answers with its own words and stories. Comparing does not mean ranking.

words.d: to look at how two or more things are alike and different
choosing not to use force or harm

look.title: Three Answers
look.text: Question: What happens because of what we do? A Hindu might say: our karma shapes our next life. A Buddhist might say: craving and actions keep the cycle of suffering going. A Jain might say: harmful actions bind karma to the soul.
look.prompt: How are these three answers alike? How is the Jain answer different?

check.q: How do Jains describe karma?

check.why: Jains picture karma as fine matter that binds to the soul.

check.q: Which leader learned from Jain ideas about non-violence?
check.why: Gandhi, a Hindu, was influenced by Jain ideas of ahimsa.

check.q: What is a fair way to compare traditions?
choices: ask each the same question and describe its answer
count which is oldest and pick it
check.why: Scholars compare by describing each answer without ranking.

lessons.title: Confucius and Respect
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught respect for parents and teachers and kindness as the base of a good society.
reading: *Confucius* lived in China about 2,500 years ago. His Chinese name is Kongzi, which means Master Kong. He was a teacher. He believed a peaceful society starts with good families and good leaders. After he died, his students wrote down his sayings in the *Analects*.

Confucius taught *filial piety*. That means respect and care for parents and grandparents. He also taught respect for teachers and elders. He said leaders should be good examples, not bullies. Good manners and rituals help people live well together, he taught.

Confucius's most important value is often called ren. Ren means kindness or humaneness toward others. Many families in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam still honor his ideas. Some call Confucianism a religion; others call it a way of life.

words.d: the book of Confucius's sayings, written down by his students
respect and care for parents and elders
a Chinese teacher who lived about 2,500 years ago

check.why: His students wrote down his sayings in the Analects.

lessons.title: The Dao: The Way of Nature
lessons.mainIdea: Daoists try to live in harmony with the Dao, the natural way of all things.
reading: Daoism is an ancient tradition from China. Its best-known book is the *Daodejing*. Tradition says a wise man named Laozi wrote it. Scholars are not sure who wrote it or when. It is short and full of poems about the Dao.

*Dao* means the way. Daoists describe the Dao as the natural flow behind all things. They say it cannot be fully put into words. Daoists try to live simply and not force things. They learn from water, which is soft but can wear away rock.

The yin-yang symbol comes from Chinese thought. It is a circle of dark and light that fit together. *Yin* and *yang* are opposites that need each other, like night and day. Many Daoists believe health and peace come from keeping them in balance.

words.d: "the way"; in Daoism, the natural flow behind all things
the best-known Daoist book, linked by tradition to Laozi
two opposite forces that need each other and stay in balance

look.title: Be Like Water
look.text: The best way to live is like water. Water helps all things and does not fight with them. It goes to low places others avoid.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 8, in our own words
look.prompt: What does water teach, according to this passage?

check.q: What does the word Dao mean?
check.why: Dao means the way, the natural flow of things.

check.q: What do yin and yang show?

check.why: Yin and yang are paired opposites in balance.

check.q: Why do Daoists learn from water?

check.why: The Daodejing praises water for helping without fighting.

lessons.title: Lunar New Year and Blended Ways
lessons.mainIdea: Lunar New Year and ancestor honoring show how many people in East Asia blend several traditions.
reading: *Lunar New Year* falls in late January or February. It follows the moon. Families clean the house to sweep out bad luck. They share big meals and give red envelopes with money to children. Each year is named for one of twelve animals, like the dragon or the rabbit.

During the new year, many families honor their *ancestors*. Ancestors are family members who lived long ago. People may set out food or burn incense before family pictures. This practice is linked to Confucian respect for family.

In China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, many people follow more than one tradition. A family might honor ancestors in a Confucian way, visit a Buddhist temple and use Daoist ideas about balance. Many people there do not see this as a problem. Chicago's Chinatown celebrates the new year with a parade.

words.d: a new year festival that follows the moon, celebrated in much of East Asia
a family member who lived long ago
